PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE WHOLESALE                             §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
AND IOU RETAIL TRANSMISSION COST                           §        OF TEXAS
RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT REGION                               §

COMMENTS OF FEDOR MIKHEEV, TEXAS A&M UNIVERSITY ENERGY
INSTITUTE

Fedor Mikheev files these comments in an individual capacity on the proposal for publication of
amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code §§ 25.192 and 25.193 and new § 25.252,
approved by the Commission at its July 9, 2026 open meeting. The views expressed are my own
and do not represent the positions of Texas A&M University, the Texas A&M Energy Institute,
or any research sponsor.
I bring twenty years of technical and commercial experience in energy equipment and capital
projects with major international energy service companies, working with upstream and
midstream operators across multiple geographies. That work concerns how operators commit to
and unwind capital and production plans, and the rotating equipment, compression, and
winterization systems that determine what a facility can physically do on a given notice period. I
now apply that experience to research conducted at the Texas A&M Energy Institute, whose
faculty review and analytical resources support the quantitative work underlying these
comments. I am the first author of a study of multi-utility coordination in the Port Houston
Baytown-La Porte corridor.1
That study reconstructs from public data how a cluster of twelve petrochemical, refining, and
industrial-gas anchors responds to the price and cost-allocation signals this rulemaking would
change. Transmission cost allocation is not a peripheral input to it: under the current four
coincident peak (4CP) methodology it accounts for approximately $25.0 million per year – 27%
of the corridor’s $93.7 million mean modeled annual coordination value.2 I have also filed
comments in Project No. 58482 on the proposed Large Load Demand Management Service.
Two classes of claim appear in what follows and the Commission should weigh them differently.
The quantitative claims – the corridor baseline, the composition of the value at stake, and the
effect of the proposed Minimum Billing Demand on it – rest on a methodology built entirely
from public sources; I offer Commission Staff a technical briefing on request, so that the
derivation can be walked through in detail. The operating claims – what a notice period means
against a committed plan, how freeze protection and minimum-flow systems behave in sustained
cold, and what determines electrical load composition at compression-driven facilities – rest on
two decades of equipment and capital-project work with operators, supplemented, where the

 question concerns downstream chemical processes specifically, by the engineering literature and
by the faculty review supporting the study. Where a recommendation rests on the second, I say
so.

These comments proceed from a single principle: a large load customer should be charged for
the system capacity it causes to be built, net of the capacity it verifiably relieves. The proposed
rule gives careful effect to the first half of that principle. My comments are directed principally
to the second, which the rule does not yet reach. As drafted, a large load customer that reduces
demand – including on ERCOT’s own instruction under the service the Commission is
simultaneously creating in Project No. 58482 – receives no transmission-cost recognition for the
reduction at either the retail or the wholesale level.

I. Summary of Position
I support the replacement of the 4CP methodology with a 12CP methodology, the codification of
a 30-minute measurement interval, and the requirement that non-IOU distribution service
providers give ERCOT access to settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer.
Each is a material improvement.
I support the objective of the large load Minimum Billing Demand. Capacity that a customer
reserves, causes to be built, and does not use should be paid for by the customer that reserved it.
That is a real problem and the Commission is right to address it.
I identify one drafting defect and one policy conflict in the Minimum Billing Demand as
proposed. The defect is that proposed § 25.193(d)(2)(C) appears to have no operative effect. The
conflict is that the Minimum Billing Demand, combined with the wholesale adjustment in
proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B), eliminates the transmission-cost consequence of demand reduction
for the entire population of § 25.194 large load customers – including reductions the
Commission proposes to purchase with up to $54 million per year of ratepayer funds under
PURA § 39.170(b).
Both items are correctable without disturbing the objective, and my recommendations are
directed to that end.

II. The 12CP Signal Is Nullified for the Customers the Reform Targets
A. Proposed § 25.193(d)(2)(C) appears to have no operative effect.
Proposed § 25.193(d)(2) sets the large load Minimum Billing Demand at the greater of (A)
contracted peak demand, (B) the highest non-coincident peak demand placed on the system in
the past year, or (C) the customer's 12CP demand.
Subparagraph (C) is circular. Under proposed § 25.193(c), the Minimum Billing Demand is
substituted for a large load customer's actual 12CP demand where the latter is the lesser of the
two. The 12CP demand is thus the billing determinant that the floor replaces. Including it as a
prong of the floor cannot raise the floor above the value being replaced; at most it returns that
value unchanged.
Subparagraph (C) is also dominated by subparagraph (B) wherever the two are measured over
the same period. The 12CP demand is the average of twelve coincident values, each of which is
by definition no greater than the maximum demand placed on the system in that period. Their
average is therefore no greater than that maximum, with equality only where the customer's
demand at all twelve intervals equals its annual maximum. That equality case is not hypothetical


                                                2
 and will be approached by a high-load-factor customer, but it produces a tie rather than a binding
value.
I note one qualification, which on examination does not appear to disturb the conclusion.
Subparagraph (B) is measured over "the past year," a period the rule does not define, while
subparagraph (C) is keyed to the most recent ERCOT 12CP intervals, which § 25.192 defines as
October 1 through September 30. Where those windows diverge, a customer whose demand falls
materially after the 12CP window could in principle produce a subparagraph (C) value exceeding
subparagraph (B). Subparagraph (C) would still have to exceed subparagraph (A) to become
operative, however, and subparagraph (A) is contracted peak demand, which § 25.193(d)(3) fixes
for not less than twenty years and which accordingly does not decline as the load declines. A
customer's 12CP demand can exceed its contracted peak only where it has drawn more than it
contracted for. Prong (C) therefore remains inoperative in the divergence case as well.
Recommendation: define the subparagraph (B) measurement period. Subparagraph (B)
refers to the highest non-coincident peak demand placed on the system "in the past year." The
rule does not indicate whether that is a calendar year, a rate year corresponding to the October 1
through September 30 window used for the ERCOT 12CP intervals, or a rolling twelve months
from the billing date. Those produce different floors for the same customer, and because
subparagraph (B) sets the floor wherever it exceeds contracted peak demand, the difference is
not immaterial. Aligning the period with the § 25.192 twelve-interval window would have the
further benefit of placing subparagraphs (B) and (C) on a common measurement basis.

B. The consequence is that the 12CP signal does not survive the floor.
The stated purpose of moving from 4CP to 12CP is to give customers a price signal reflecting
their contribution to system peaks across the full year rather than four summer intervals. For load
subject to the Minimum Billing Demand, that signal does not survive.
Because the floor is the greater of contracted peak demand and prior-year highest non-coincident
peak demand, a customer whose 12CP demand sits at or below it (which is any customer
consuming within its contracted capacity) is billed the same whether it curtails during all twelve
ERCOT 12CP intervals or during none. Two features reinforce the result. Subparagraph (B)
measures non-coincident demand, so curtailing at the twelve coincident intervals does not lower
the following year's floor either. And subparagraph (A) is fixed for no less than twenty years
under proposed § 25.193(d)(3), with 240 consecutive payments required under proposed §
25.252(e)(2)(ii).
The signal survives only where a customer's 12CP demand exceeds both its contracted peak and
its prior-year maximum, and it is extinguished as soon as demand returns to the floor. That is not
the operating range to which this rule is addressed.
Proposed § 25.193(d)(1) charges the REP serving the large load customer rather than the
customer directly, so whether the result reaches the customer depends on the retail contract.
Where transmission costs are passed through as incurred, as is customary in large load service, it
passes through with them.

C. The nullification is complete, because it operates at the wholesale level as well.
Proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B) requires ERCOT to adjust each DSP 12CP load value by adding, for
each large load customer of that DSP, the difference between that customer’s Minimum Billing
Demand and its measured 12CP load. The customer’s actual demand reduction is therefore added
back before the DSP’s wholesale allocation is computed. There is no level of the transmission



                                                3
 cost recovery system at which a § 25.194 large load customer’s demand reduction is visible. The
effect is not merely that the customer captures no benefit. Because the adjustment holds the
adjusted DSP 12CP load constant, the ERCOT 12CP denominator, the resulting transmission
rate, and the DSP's allocation are all unchanged by the reduction. No other load benefits from it
either. The demand reduction is not redistributed within the transmission cost recovery system; it
is removed from it.
Recommendation: conform § 25.192(f)(1)(B) to § 25.193(c). Section 25.193(c) applies the
Minimum Billing Demand only "where that customer's 12CP demand is less than" the Minimum
Billing Demand. Section 25.192(f)(1)(B) contains no equivalent condition, so where a customer's
measured 12CP load exceeds its Minimum Billing Demand the adjustment is negative and
reduces the DSP's allocated load below the level measured. The Commission should add the
same condition or provide that the adjustment may not be less than zero.

III. Reconciliation with PURA § 39.170(b) and Project No. 58482
In Project No. 58482 the Commission has proposed new § 25.521, implementing PURA §
39.170(b). Under that rule ERCOT will procure demand reductions from qualifying large load
customers, paying the qualified scheduling entity that represents them, for deployment when an
energy emergency alert event arising from extreme weather is anticipated or underway.
A large load customer subject to § 25.194 may participate in that service. If it does, and reduces
demand on ERCOT's instruction, the reduction is added back under proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B)
and the customer's transmission cost allocation is computed as though it had remained on the
system.
The difficulty is one of cost causation. Transmission costs are allocated on coincident peak
demand because coincident peak is what drives network sizing. A customer that is not drawing at
the coincident interval, because ERCOT directed it not to be, did not contribute to the peak that
drives the allocation. The legitimate purpose of the Minimum Billing Demand, recovering the
network investment built to serve reserved capacity, is already accomplished by subparagraph
(A), which fixes the floor at contracted peak for twenty years. Extending the floor to override
measured coincident behavior serves a different purpose, and the reserved-capacity rationale
does not reach it. Whatever the merits of the Minimum Billing Demand as applied to idle
reserved capacity, it should not apply to capacity the Commission has instructed the customer to
release.
There is a serious objection to any exclusion, and it should be stated before it is answered. A
Minimum Billing Demand is designed to be insensitive to behavior. That insensitivity is the
point, because a floor that moves with measured demand is not a floor at all, and every carve-out
reopens to some degree the measurement question the provision was meant to close.
The answer is that the exclusion proposed here is bounded by an external event rather than by the
customer's own election. A customer cannot place itself inside it. The reduction must be
instructed by ERCOT, or occur under a protocol or service ERCOT administers, and the affected
intervals are identifiable from ERCOT's deployment records rather than from the customer's
assertion. That is a different thing from a floor that yields to demand generally. It leaves the
provision fully effective against the behavior it targets, which is capacity reserved and simply not
used, while removing its effect where the reduction was directed rather than chosen.

Recommendation 1 – Exclude verified reliability-driven demand reduction from the
Minimum Billing Demand and from the § 25.192(f)(1)(B) adjustment. Specifically, an


                                                 4
 interval in which a large load customer’s demand was reduced pursuant to any of the following
should be excluded from the determination of its highest non-coincident peak demand and from
the wholesale add-back:
(i) deployment of, or an availability obligation or qualification test under, the Large Load
      Demand Management Service established under PURA § 39.170(b);
(ii) a curtailment protocol developed under PURA § 39.170(a);
(iii) an ERCOT-procured reliability service or ancillary service; or
(iv) a firm load shed instruction issued by ERCOT or by the customer’s transmission or
      distribution service provider.
Each is verifiable from ERCOT deployment records and settlement meter data, so the exclusion
is administrable rather than self-certified. The carve-out does not weaken the Minimum Billing
Demand as applied to its intended target: a customer that simply does not energize reserved
capacity has no ERCOT deployment record to point to and remains fully subject to the floor.
(v) the recovery period following any reduction described in subparagraphs (i) through (iv), for
      such reasonable interval as ERCOT determines is required to restore normal operation.
A curtailment instruction reduces demand, but the recovery from it may not. Re-establishing
minimum flows and restarting compression and pumping duty can transiently exceed steady-
state demand, and under proposed § 25.193(d)(2)(B) that transient would set the customer's
Minimum Billing Demand for the following twelve months. A rule that exposed a participant to
a twelve-month increase in its transmission floor because of having performed would not survive
contact with the operators it is meant to recruit.

Recommendation 2 – Characterize response to the 12CP methodology this rule creates. A
customer that reduces demand at a 12CP interval is responding to an allocation rule that assigns
fixed network costs based on measured demand at twelve administratively determined intervals.
It is not responding to the marginal value of energy: it curtails at the predicted coincident peak
whether the settlement point price at that interval is high or low, and it would not curtail at an
equally high price occurring outside those intervals.
That characterization matters beyond this docket. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) disqualifies from the
Large Load Demand Management Service any large load customer "that curtails in response to
the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by" ERCOT. The proposed rule in Project No.
58482 reaches enrollment in a demand response program and so, on its face, would not capture
self-directed 12CP management. The exposure lies in the implementing test ERCOT is directed
to apply. I respectfully recommend that the Commission direct that test to distinguish response to
a transmission cost allocation methodology from response to a settlement point price.
I note the argument, made in Project No. 58482, that a load capable of coincident-peak response
has demonstrated a capability to respond to price and should be treated accordingly. The
Commission's authority to direct the content of that test does not appear to be in question. PURA
§ 39.151, which Staff cite in the Statutory Authority for this proposal, grants the Commission
complete oversight of ERCOT. PURA § 39.170(b) separately directs the Commission to require
ERCOT to develop the service and to make the rules governing it, including the eligibility
conditions in subsection (b)(3). Specifying how the price responsiveness test distinguishes cost
allocation response from settlement price response is therefore an exercise of the authority under
which the service is being established, rather than a substitution of the Commission's judgment
for a determination the Legislature reserved to ERCOT. The statute does not disqualify a
customer that is capable of price response; it disqualifies one that curtails in response to price.



                                                5
 Every large flexible load is capable of price response – that capability is the reason the service is
worth procuring. A test built on capability rather than conduct would disqualify substantially the
entire eligible population and leave the service without participants.

IV. Responses to Staff’s Specific Questions
QUESTION NO. 1: Should the values associated with the large load Minimum Billing
Demand provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak
demands or different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

RESPONSE: Yes. I would respectfully suggest that the most useful differentiator is the
relationship between contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand, rather than
either quantity taken alone.
If the objective is to recover network capacity that a customer reserved, caused to be built, and
does not use, then utilization is what identifies that capacity, and magnitude on its own does not.
A 500 MW customer whose highest non-coincident demand reaches 480 MW leaves 20 MW
unused. A 100 MW customer reaching 40 MW leaves 60 MW, three times as much at one fifth
the size.
As proposed, the floor resolves to contracted peak demand in both cases, so a customer that
reserved accurately and one that over-reserved substantially receive the same treatment. The
Commission may wish to consider whether that is the intended result, since the two differ
precisely on the dimension the provision is directed at. This concerns transmission planning.
Resource adequacy is addressed separately in response to Question No. 6, where the conclusion
differs for reasons given there.
I offer this as a refinement rather than a substitute for a uniform percentage. Modeling filed in
this proceeding on July 30 applies a single Minimum Billing Demand level across new large
loads and quantifies the level at which existing customers are held harmless. That approach has
the considerable advantages of being administrable and of resting on analysis the Commission
can examine. A utilization-differentiated floor would track cost causation more closely, but it
would require the Commission to calibrate a second parameter without comparable modeling
before it. If a uniform percentage is adopted, the observations above may still assist in setting it,
since the customers who bear it most heavily will be those whose utilization is lowest, which is
the intended effect.3
A second dimension may also be worth attention, with one distinction that seems important to
preserve. Where curtailability is a condition of interconnection, as under the protocols required
by PURA § 39.170(a), the capacity that must be planned and built to serve the customer is
genuinely smaller, and there is a good case for recognizing that in the floor. Voluntary
emergency response under PURA § 39.170(b) sits differently, because transmission planning
serves firm peak demand and a product deployed on 24-hour notice for a limited number of
hours does not reduce the peak a planner must serve. The two are probably better handled
separately: mandatory curtailability through the floor, since it is a permanent characteristic of the
interconnection, and voluntary response through the exclusion discussed in Part III.

                                                          6
 Either would be measurable from the settlement quality meter data this rule would require, and
as readily verified for a portfolio of co-located customers under a common qualified scheduling
entity as for a single site.


QUESTION NO. 2: Should the large load Minimum Billing Demand be (a) fixed for 20
years as proposed, (b) reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or (c) extended to a
longer time period?

RESPONSE: Option (b) – reduced in phases, though for a different reason than the passage of
time alone.
Two features of the proposal deserve acknowledgment before any change is suggested. Section
25.252(c)(3) requires an interconnection agreement with a term of not less than 20 years, so the
20-year period in § 25.193(d)(3) and the 240 payments required by § 25.252(e)(2)(ii) are
symmetric with the commitment the customer makes. And § 25.252(c)(2) already requires the
customer to fund interconnection costs through contribution in aid of construction, in cash, so the
Minimum Billing Demand is not carrying that cost; it is allocating general network transmission
cost against reserved capacity. On both points the proposal is internally coherent, and the case
for phasing does not depend on either being wrong.
The case rests on information. At the point of interconnection the Commission cannot know
whether a customer will grow into its reservation. Five years later there is an operating record
that answers the question. A floor fixed for the full term sets the charge on the least informed
estimate available and never revisits it, even where subsequent measurement shows the
reservation to have been substantially larger than the load.
The record now contains support for a shorter period. Net present value analysis filed in this
proceeding indicates that an obligation period of approximately thirteen years at a floor of 75
percent of contracted demand, or approximately nine years at 80 percent, is sufficient for
revenues from new large loads to exceed the incremental transmission costs incurred to serve
them, and that at those levels existing customers are held harmless or better off. The Commission
will want to test those figures. If they hold, the question becomes where within a shorter band the
obligation should fall, rather than whether twenty years at full contracted peak is required.4
A phased floor would let the charge converge on demonstrated behavior while preserving the
early-period protection that justifies the provision. The Commission may wish to consider
pairing any step-down with relinquishment of the corresponding capacity, so that a customer's
obligation falls only where the reserved capability it is no longer paying for returns to the
system. PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish uniform requirements for
determining when capacity subject to an outstanding financial commitment may be reallocated,
and proposed § 25.252(d)(2) is the closest existing analogue at the tariff level, though it
addresses reallocation on a customer’s failure to meet requirements rather than voluntary
relinquishment and would need to be broadened accordingly. The mechanism is therefore not
merely available; the Legislature has directed that it exist.
I would not recommend option (c). Extending the obligation beyond the minimum agreement
term would separate the payment from the commitment that justifies it, and the symmetry
described above seems worth preserving.

 QUESTION NO. 3: Should the large load Minimum Billing Demand be based on some
measure of demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand – a “ratcheted”
demand, or a “weighted average” of contracted peak or highest NCP and 12CP demand?

RESPONSE: Of the two alternatives, I would suggest the ratcheted percentage is the safer
structure, and that the weighted average is preferable only if paired with relinquishment.
The difficulty with the weighted average as posed is that it gives the largest reduction to the
customer that uses the least. On an illustrative 500 MW reservation, with the reference weight
declining from 100 percent to 35 percent over eight years, a customer that ramps to 95 percent
utilization would see its floor fall from 500 MW to roughly 484 MW, while a customer that
never energizes would see its floor fall to roughly 175 MW. The customer whose behavior the
provision is directed at receives a two thirds reduction; the customer using its reservation as
intended receives almost none. Any formula converging on measured demand shares this
property, because the customer with no measured demand converges fastest.
The ratchet does not have that difficulty, since it applies the same percentage to every customer.
Its weakness is the opposite: being indifferent to utilization, it under-collects from the customer
using its reservation and still over-collects from the customer that is not. That is the lesser
problem, and it is the one the Commission has modeling before it to calibrate. Analysis filed in
this proceeding models levels between 60 and 100 percent of contracted demand and identifies
approximately 75 percent as rate-neutral for existing customers, with 80 percent producing a
reduction in their rates and 70 percent or below shifting costs to other classes. That lower
boundary is worth noting, because transmission cost of service is fixed and any reduction in large
load billing determinants is borne by someone else.5
If the Commission prefers the weighted average, the condition that makes it workable is
relinquishment. Where convergence toward measured demand is available only to a customer
that permanently releases the corresponding reserved capacity, the formula stops rewarding
under-use and instead prices an exit from over-reservation. That pairing also gives effect to
PURA § 37.0561, which directs the Commission to establish uniform requirements for
determining when capacity subject to an outstanding financial commitment may be reallocated.
Proposed § 25.252(d)(2) supplies the closest tariff mechanism, though it reaches reallocation on
default rather than voluntary relinquishment and would need broadening. What is missing is the
rate consequence that would give a customer a reason to use it.
Whichever structure is chosen, I would suggest the level matters more than the form. Analysis in
this proceeding observes that a large load's incentive to curtail during periods of grid stress
weakens as the floor rises, and breaks down somewhere in the range of 85 to 90 percent of
contracted demand, because the load forgoes more in operating revenue than it saves in avoided
transmission cost. The floor proposed here sits above that range. Because § 25.193(d)(2) sets the
minimum at the greater of contracted peak demand and prior year non-coincident peak demand,
it operates at effectively 100 percent of contracted capacity for any customer consuming within
its contract, and as described in Part II the curtailment signal at that level is not merely weakened
but absent.6

 On how any decline should be structured, I would suggest keying it to demonstrated utilization
rather than elapsed time, for the reasons given in response to Question No. 1, subject to a time-
based floor.
One further condition applies to either alternative. The measured component should exclude
intervals in which demand was reduced pursuant to a reliability instruction, for the reasons
discussed in Part III, with excluded intervals replaced by the average of the remaining intervals
in the measurement period. Without that exclusion either formulation would penalize
performance under the programs the Commission is establishing, and a ratchet keyed to prior
year non-coincident demand would do so most sharply, since it carries a single interval into the
following year.

QUESTION NO. 4: Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational
load, defined as an entity subject to § 25.194 in which 50% or greater of the demand at the
site consists of power electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data
centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities?

RESPONSE: I would respectfully suggest separate rate treatment is not necessary, because the
characteristic that distinguishes these loads is already addressed by the Minimum Billing
Demand, on a basis that does not require classifying customers by end use. The record in this
proceeding supports that conclusion from a different direction. The modeling filed here
addresses the cost-shifting concern associated with new large load using a single instrument
applied uniformly to loads above 75 megawatts, and reaches a calibrated result without reference
at any point to what the load is used for. If the protective objective can be met on a technology-
neutral basis, and the analysis before the Commission suggests it can, the case for a further
classification defined by end use is correspondingly weaker.7
From a transmission cost perspective, computational load is not unusual in the ways the
proposed definition captures. A high load factor makes a data center an intensive user of network
capability per megawatt reserved, which is ordinarily a favorable characteristic. What sets these
loads apart in the Commission's recent experience is the gap between capacity reserved and
capacity used, and the speculative pattern of interconnection requests that produces it. That is a
reservation behavior rather than a technology, and the provisions proposed here address it
directly.
The proposed criterion would also reach loads it is not aimed at. A threshold of 50 percent or
greater power electronic based demand does not isolate computation. Electrolytic processes are
served through rectifiers and are almost entirely power electronic, chlor-alkali production being
the clearest case. Electric arc and induction processes are power electronic by construction.
Electric drive compression, increasingly specified at midstream gas facilities in place of gas
turbine and reciprocating drivers, is variable frequency drive served, and at such a site
compression is the dominant load. Each is an established industrial process with no
computational element, and each is represented in the load growth this rule will govern.
ERCOT's long-term load forecast segments projected large load into cryptocurrency mining, data
center (non-crypto), industrial including hydrogen and e-fuels, and oil and gas covering chemical
refining, production, and processing. The industrial and oil and gas categories are each projected
to reach the low thousands of megawatts by 2030. Whether any facility crosses 50 percent is a


7
    Supra note 3.


                                                9
 measurement question I do not attempt to answer, and it would vary site by site. The point is that
the criterion is not selective for the loads the question describes.8
On the legal support the Commission has requested, PURA § 36.001 authorizes the Commission
to establish and regulate the rates of an electric utility and to adopt rules determining the
classification of customers and services and the applicability of rates. The question is therefore
not whether the Commission may classify, but on what basis. PURA § 36.003(b) requires that a
rate not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory, and that it be sufficient,
equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. Section 36.003(c)(3) provides
that an electric utility may not establish or maintain an unreasonable difference concerning rates
between classes of service. These provisions apply here because § 25.193 governs the rates of
investor-owned distribution service providers, over which the Commission has exclusive original
jurisdiction under PURA § 32.001.
The operative word in each provision is "unreasonable." Differences between classes are
contemplated; differences unrelated to the cost of providing service are what the statute reaches.
A criterion defined by the proportion of a site's demand served through power electronics does
not track cost of service, as it would group an electrolytic hydrogen facility with a data center on
the strength of a shared conversion technology, while leaving reservation behavior, utilization,
and interconnection history, which are the characteristics that bear on cost, outside the definition.
Because the criterion reaches only entities subject to § 25.194, the concern is not with the
existing industrial fleet but with new interconnections: hydrogen electrolysis, new chlor-alkali
capacity, and electric drive compression at new midstream facilities are each substantially power
electronic and none is computational.
I would add one structural observation. PURA § 37.0561 defines "large load customer," so the
class to which the Minimum Billing Demand applies has a statutory foundation. A "large
computational load" subclass would rest on the Commission's own line drawing, and would
accordingly carry a heavier justification burden under § 36.003 than the class the Legislature has
already defined. I offer this as an identification of the provisions that appear to bear on the
question rather than as a legal opinion.

QUESTION NO. 5: Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be
broadened to include transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch
study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

RESPONSE: Yes in part, and I would respectfully suggest the qualification matters more than
the answer.
It is worth noting at the outset what a broadened definition carries with it. Proposed §
25.252(c)(2) requires a large load customer to fund transmission interconnection costs through
contribution in aid of construction, in direct cash, with an allowance prohibited. Expanding the

The 4CP methodology allocates transmission cost on the basis of demand during four intervals
occurring in June through September. It was designed when ERCOT's reliability risk was
predominantly a summer afternoon phenomenon. The February 2021 winter event, and the
winter-peaking risk that has driven much of the Commission's subsequent reliability work, fall

I would add one observation about the design of any winter component, which bears on the point

window is materially harder for a continuous process facility than a fixed monthly interval.
Readiness must be maintained across the whole window rather than prepared for a known date,
and for loads whose winter flexibility depends on freeze protection, heat tracing, and minimum
flow systems, that is an operating posture rather than a scheduling decision. A design that suits

response from process industry. If the Commission adopts floating winter intervals, I would
suggest pairing them with advance notification of the window in which they may fall.
I offer one observation drawn from equipment and capital-project work on gas processing and
compression facilities, where winterization is a governing design constraint, which I have not
seen addressed in the comments I have reviewed. Winter curtailment at a continuous process is
qualitatively harder than summer curtailment, not merely more frequent. Summer peak shaving
is typically achieved by reducing electrically driven compression, pumping, and air separation
duty for a short interval while the process remains within stable operating envelopes. Winter
electrical load at the same class of facility includes freeze protection, heat tracing, and minimum-
flow circulation, systems that exist precisely to prevent the freeze-off, loss-of-containment, and
restart hazards the February 2021 event made vivid across the Texas gas supply chain. Curtailing
those loads is a different exercise, and doing it safely is an engineering question rather than a
scheduling one. The point is not specific to any one process; it follows from the function those
systems perform.
The consequence is not that the winter intervals are unfair. A facility that cannot safely reduce
those loads will not reduce them, will contribute to the winter peak, and will pay its share of it,
which is the result cost causation calls for. The consequence is that the Commission should
expect the demand response elicited by the winter intervals to develop more slowly, and to come
disproportionately from loads whose flexibility is electrical rather than thermal. Data centers and
similar loads can shift within a winter peak interval on notice. A continuous process facility can
do so only after engineering work that in many cases has not been done, because until now there
has been no price signal to justify it.

prepare a safe winter turndown needs more notice to do so than one shedding compression duty
on a hot afternoon.

In Proj ect No. 58482 the Commission has proposed new § 25.521, implementing PURA §

energy emergency alert event arising from extreme weather is anticipated or underway.

demand on ERCOT's instruction, the reduction is added back under proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B)

The difficulty is one of cost causation. Transmission costs are allocated on coincident peak
demand because coincident peak is what drives network sizing. A customer that is not drawing at
the coincident interval, because ERCOT directed it not to be, did not contribute to the peak that
drives the allocation. The legitimate purpose of the Minimum Billing Demand, recovering the
network investment built to serve reserved capacity, is already accomplished by subparagraph

measured coincident behavior serves a different purpose, and the reserved-capacity rationale
does not reach it. Whatever the merits of the Minimum Billing Demand as applied to idle
reserved capacity, it should not apply to capacity the Commission has instructed the customer to
release.
There is a serious objection to any exclusion, and it should be stated before it is answered. A
Minimum Billing Demand is designed to be insensitive to behavior. That insensitivity is the
point, because a floor that moves with measured demand is not a floor at all, and every carve-out
reopens to some degree the measurement question the provision was meant to close.
The answer is that the exclusion proposed here is bounded by an external event rather than by the
customer's own election. A customer cannot place itself inside it. The reduction must be
instructed by ERCOT, or occur under a protocol or service ERCOT administers, and the affected
intervals are identifiable from ERCOT's deployment records rather than from the customer's
assertion. That is a different thing from a floor that yields to demand generally. It leaves the
provision fully effective against the behavior it targets, which is capacity reserved and simply not
used, while removing its effect where the reduction was directed rather than chosen.

QUESTION NO. 1: Should the values associated with the large load Minimum Billing
Demand provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak
demands or different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

RESPONSE: Yes. I would respectfully suggest that the most useful differentiator is the
relationship between contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand, rather than
either quantity taken alone.
If the obj ective is to recover network capacity that a customer reserved, caused to be built, and
does not use, then utilization is what identifies that capacity, and magnitude on its own does not.
A 500 MW customer whose highest non-coincident demand reaches 480 MW leaves 20 MW
unused. A 100 MW customer reaching 40 MW leaves 60 MW, three times as much at one fifth
the size.
As proposed, the floor resolves to contracted peak demand in both cases, so a customer that
reserved accurately and one that over-reserved substantially receive the same treatment. The
Commission may wish to consider whether that is the intended result, since the two differ
precisely on the dimension the provision is directed at. This concerns transmission planning.
Resource adequacy is addressed separately in response to Question No. 6, where the conclusion
differs for reasons given there.
I offer this as a refinement rather than a substitute for a uniform percentage. Modeling filed in
this proceeding on July 30 applies a single Minimum Billing Demand level across new large
loads and quantifies the level at which existing customers are held harmless. That approach has
the considerable advantages of being administrable and of resting on analysis the Commission
can examine. A utilization-differentiated floor would track cost causation more closely, but it
would require the Commission to calibrate a second parameter without comparable modeling
before it. If a uniform percentage is adopted, the observations above may still assist in setting it,
since the customers who bear it most heavily will be those whose utilization is lowest, which is
the intended effect. 3
A second dimension may also be worth attention, with one distinction that seems important to
preserve. Where curtailability is a condition of interconnection, as under the protocols required
by PURA § 39.170(a), the capacity that must be planned and built to serve the customer is
genuinely smaller, and there is a good case for recognizing that in the floor. Voluntary
emergency response under PURA § 39. 170(b) sits differently, because transmission planning
serves firm peak demand and a product deployed on 24-hour notice for a limited number of
hours does not reduce the peak a planner must serve. The two are probably better handled
separately: mandatory curtailability through the floor, since it is a permanent characteristic of the
interconnection, and voluntary response through the exclusion discussed in Part III.

QUESTION NO. 2: Should the large load Minimum Billing Demand be (a) fixed for 20
years as proposed, (b) reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or (c) extended to a
longer time period?

RESPONSE: Option (b) - reduced in phases, though for a different reason than the passage of
time alone.
Two features of the proposal deserve acknowledgment before any change is suggested. Section
25.252(c)(3) requires an interconnection agreement with a term of not less than 20 years, so the
20-year period in § 25.193(d)(3) and the 240 payments required by § 25.252(e)(2)(ii) are
symmetric with the commitment the customer makes. And § 25.252(c)(2) already requires the
customer to fund interconnection costs through contribution in aid of construction, in cash, so the
Minimum Billing Demand is not carrying that cost; it is allocating general network transmission
cost against reserved capacity. On both points the proposal is internally coherent, and the case
for phasing does not depend on either being wrong.
The case rests on information. At the point of interconnection the Commission cannot know
whether a customer will grow into its reservation. Five years later there is an operating record
that answers the question. A floor fixed for the full term sets the charge on the least informed
estimate available and never revisits it, even where subsequent measurement shows the
reservation to have been substantially larger than the load.
The record now contains support for a shorter period. Net present value analysis filed in this
proceeding indicates that an obligation period of approximately thirteen years at a floor of 75
percent of contracted demand, or approximately nine years at 80 percent, is sufficient for
revenues from new large loads to exceed the incremental transmission costs incurred to serve
them, and that at those levels existing customers are held harmless or better off. The Commission
will want to test those figures. If they hold, the question becomes where within a shorter band the
obligation should fall, rather than whether twenty years at full contracted peak is required.4
A phased floor would let the charge converge on demonstrated behavior while preserving the
early-period protection that justifies the provision. The Commission may wish to consider
pairing any step-down with relinquishment of the corresponding capacity, so that a customer's

determining when capacity subj ect to an outstanding financial commitment may be reallocated,
and proposed § 25.252(d)(2) is the closest existing analogue at the tariff level, though it
addresses reallocation on a customer' s failure to meet requirements rather than voluntary
relinquishment and would need to be broadened accordingly. The mechanism is therefore not
merely available; the Legislature has directed that it exist.
I would not recommend option (c). Extending the obligation beyond the minimum agreement
term would separate the payment from the commitment that justifies it, and the symmetry
described above seems worth preserving.

measure of demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand - a "ratcheted"
demand, or a "weighted average" of contracted peak or highest NCP and 12CP demand?

RESPONSE: Of the two alternatives, I would suggest the ratcheted percentage is the safer
structure, and that the weighted average is preferable only if paired with relinquishment.
The difficulty with the weighted average as posed is that it gives the largest reduction to the
customer that uses the least. On an illustrative 500 MW reservation, with the reference weight
declining from 100 percent to 35 percent over eight years, a customer that ramps to 95 percent
utilization would see its floor fall from 500 MW to roughly 484 MW, while a customer that
never energizes would see its floor fall to roughly 175 MW. The customer whose behavior the
provision is directed at receives a two thirds reduction; the customer using its reservation as
intended receives almost none. Any formula converging on measured demand shares this
property, because the customer with no measured demand converges fastest.
The ratchet does not have that difficulty, since it applies the same percentage to every customer.
Its weakness is the opposite: being indifferent to utilization, it under-collects from the customer
using its reservation and still over-collects from the customer that is not. That is the lesser
problem, and it is the one the Commission has modeling before it to calibrate. Analysis filed in
this proceeding models levels between 60 and 100 percent of contracted demand and identifies
approximately 75 percent as rate-neutral for existing customers, with 80 percent producing a
reduction in their rates and 70 percent or below shifting costs to other classes. That lower
boundary is worth noting, because transmission cost of service is fixed and any reduction in large
load billing determinants is borne by someone else.5
If the Commission prefers the weighted average, the condition that makes it workable is
relinquishment. Where convergence toward measured demand is available only to a customer
that permanently releases the corresponding reserved capacity, the formula stops rewarding
under-use and instead prices an exit from over-reservation. That pairing also gives effect to
PURA § 37.0561, which directs the Commission to establish uniform requirements for
determining when capacity subj ect to an outstanding financial commitment may be reallocated.
Proposed § 25.252(d)(2) supplies the closest tariff mechanism, though it reaches reallocation on
default rather than voluntary relinquishment and would need broadening. What is missing is the
rate consequence that would give a customer a reason to use it.
Whichever structure is chosen, I would suggest the level matters more than the form. Analysis in
this proceeding observes that a large load's incentive to curtail during periods of grid stress
weakens as the floor rises, and breaks down somewhere in the range of 85 to 90 percent of
contracted demand, because the load forgoes more in operating revenue than it saves in avoided
transmission cost. The floor proposed here sits above that range. Because § 25.193(d)(2) sets the
minimum at the greater of contracted peak demand and prior year non-coincident peak demand,
it operates at effectively 100 percent of contracted capacity for any customer consuming within
its contract, and as described in Part II the curtailment signal at that level is not merely weakened
but absent.6

The 4CP methodology allocates transmission cost on the basis of demand during four intervals
occurring in June through September. It was designed when ERCOT's reliability risk was
predominantly a summer afternoon phenomenon. The February 2021 winter event, and the
winter-peaking risk that has driven much of the Commission's subsequent reliability work, fall
entirely outside the window 4CP prices. A methodology measured across twelve monthly peaks
distributes the signal across the year and prices a customer's contribution to winter risk for the
first time. It is also coherent with the year-round structure of the reliability instruments the
Commission is building under Senate Bill 6. I support the change.
I note that alternatives have been proposed in this proceeding, replacing 4CP with eight
coincident peaks concentrated in the months of greatest system stress, on the ground that twelve
evenly distributed intervals reward curtailment in months when the system is not stressed. The
supporting data is persuasive on its own terms: across the past five years the March, April, and
November peaks have run twenty to thirty-eight percent below each year's maximum, while the
best winter month has come within ten percent of it in four years of five. If the Commission is

 drawn to a more targeted structure, the winter component is the part that carries the reliability
benefit, and the shoulder months are the part that does not. 11
I would add one observation about the design of any winter component, which bears on the point
above about what winter curtailment requires. A floating peak defined across a multi-month
window is materially harder for a continuous process facility than a fixed monthly interval.
Readiness must be maintained across the whole window rather than prepared for a known date,
and for loads whose winter flexibility depends on freeze protection, heat tracing, and minimum
flow systems, that is an operating posture rather than a scheduling decision. A design that suits
aggregated commercial and industrial load dispatched on short notice will not elicit the same
response from process industry. If the Commission adopts floating winter intervals, I would
suggest pairing them with advance notification of the window in which they may fall.
I offer one observation drawn from equipment and capital-project work on gas processing and
compression facilities, where winterization is a governing design constraint, which I have not
seen addressed in the comments I have reviewed. Winter curtailment at a continuous process is
qualitatively harder than summer curtailment, not merely more frequent. Summer peak shaving
is typically achieved by reducing electrically driven compression, pumping, and air separation
duty for a short interval while the process remains within stable operating envelopes. Winter
electrical load at the same class of facility includes freeze protection, heat tracing, and minimum-
flow circulation, systems that exist precisely to prevent the freeze-off, loss-of-containment, and
restart hazards the February 2021 event made vivid across the Texas gas supply chain. Curtailing
those loads is a different exercise, and doing it safely is an engineering question rather than a
scheduling one. The point is not specific to any one process; it follows from the function those
systems perform.
The consequence is not that the winter intervals are unfair. A facility that cannot safely reduce
those loads will not reduce them, will contribute to the winter peak, and will pay its share of it,
which is the result cost causation calls for. The consequence is that the Commission should
expect the demand response elicited by the winter intervals to develop more slowly, and to come
disproportionately from loads whose flexibility is electrical rather than thermal. Data centers and
similar loads can shift within a winter peak interval on notice. A continuous process facility can
do so only after engineering work that in many cases has not been done, because until now there
has been no price signal to justify it.
Recommendation 3 - Provide adequate lead time before the winter intervals first bind, and
support forecasting of them. I would suggest the Commission confirm the date on which the
twelve-interval measurement first applies well in advance of the first affected rate year, so that
industrial customers have a defined period in which to engineer winter-capable response rather
than encountering the obligation without one. I would also suggest that ERCOT's forward
indication of likely winter peak intervals warrants more attention than the summer equivalent.
Summer peaks are comparatively predictable from temperature and load patterns, while winter
peaks are driven by weather events with shorter and less certain warning, and a facility that must
prepare a safe winter turndown needs more notice to do so than one shedding compression duty
on a hot afternoon.

 B. The settlement-quality meter data requirement should be retained and its permitted

I support proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(A), which requires non-IOU distribution service providers to
give ERCOT timely access to settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer in their
service territory. It closes a gap in visibility that would otherwise fall unevenly across the region
depending on which entity serves a given large load. I note that jurisdictional objections have
been raised in this proceeding to other requirements the proposal places on entities that are not
investor owned. Those obj ections are directed at rate and tariff obligations rather than at data
access, and I do not read them to reach § 25.192(f)(1)(A). Should the Commission nonetheless
narrow that provision, I would suggest it identify an alternative route to the same visibility, since
interval data at each large load customer is foundational to reliability program measurement
regardless of which entity serves the customer. 12
Its value extends beyond cost allocation. Interval meter data at each large load customer is the
measurement foundation on which every demand-side instrument now before the Commission
depends. Whether a large load customer performed when instructed, whether it was available
when it said it would be, and what its demand would have been absent an instruction are all
questions answered from interval data or not answered at all. The Minimum Billing Demand
itself depends on the same source, since the comparison between contracted peak, prior year non-
coincident peak, and measured coincident demand cannot be made without it.
One point of construction is worth noting, because the provision is sometimes read more
narrowly than it reads. Subsection (f)(1)(A) requires access to settlement-quality meter data and
does not limit the granularity of that data. The thirty-minute figure codified elsewhere in §
25.192 is the aggregation window for the twelve coincident peak measurement, not a constraint
on the underlying record. That distinction matters because the reliability instruments the
Commission is establishing operate at finer resolution. In Project No. 58482 I have
recommended that the Commission permit portfolio-level participation by co-located large load
customers, with deployment performance measured against a portfolio baseline built from
settlement meter data for each participating facility. Baseline construction and baseline
variability are open design questions in that proceeding, and neither can be resolved without
settlement-quality interval data at each facility.
Recommendation 4 - Confirm that large load customer interval data may be used for
reliability program measurement. The proposed rule is silent as to permitted uses. I would
suggest the Commission confirm that data obtained under § 25.192(f)(1)(A), and large load
customer interval data generally, may be used for baseline construction and performance
verification for services established under PURA § 39.170, subject to the confidentiality
provisions of the ERCOT Protocols. I raise this as a matter of removing doubt rather than
because I am aware of any bar. The cost of confirming it now is nothing; the cost of discovering
later that the data ERCOT holds cannot be applied to the purpose for which it is needed would be
a delay in a program the Commission is separately working to stand up.

The move from 4CP to 12CP is a sound correction to a methodology that no longer reflects
where ERCOT's reliability risk falls, and the settlement-quality meter data requirement is
